options.reason: An annual injury count gives a broad measure of nonfatal harm and makes the longer-term trajectory visible.
options.answer: Recorded pedestrian injuries fell from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025 (22% lower), but rose from the 2020 low of 1,781. These are reported injury counts, not risk per pedestrian trip.

options.reason: Deaths isolate the most severe outcome and annual bars make the year-to-year toll easy to compare.
options.answer: Pedestrian deaths increased from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025 (30% higher), with substantial year-to-year variation. The count is not adjusted for pedestrian exposure.

options.metric: Brooklyn crash records with at least one pedestrian injured or killed (share)
options.denominator: All Brooklyn-assigned crash records in the same calendar year
options.reason: A crash-record share shows whether pedestrian-casualty crashes are becoming more or less common within all Brooklyn-assigned records.
options.answer: The share of Brooklyn-assigned crash records involving a pedestrian injured or killed rose from 7.4% in 2013 to 11.4% in 2025 (up 3.9 percentage points). That indicates a larger pedestrian-casualty share of recorded crashes, not exposure-adjusted risk.

answer:
[Pedestrian injuries](out/option_1.png): Reported injuries fell 22%, from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025, but rose from the 2020 low of 1,781; these counts aren’t adjusted for walking volume.
[Pedestrian deaths](out/option_2.png): Reported deaths rose 30%, from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025, so this measure shows no improvement; it isn’t adjusted for pedestrian exposure.
[Share of Brooklyn crash records with a pedestrian casualty](out/option_3.png): The share increased from 7.4% in 2013 to 11.4% in 2025, indicating a larger share of recorded crashes involved a pedestrian injured or killed, not exposure-adjusted risk.
